# OmO **Your tool for real work. But it's an agent.**
OmO is one `omo` command that turns your tokens into finished work: research across ten thousand sources, a deck people actually get, backends, frontends, code. It runs on senpi, our fork of [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), with everything below built in. ## Install ```bash curl -fsSL https://get.omo.dev/install.sh | bash omo ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://get.omo.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. The script installs the native `omo` binary for your OS and CPU into `~/.local/bin`, checks it against the release checksums, and falls back to GitHub Releases when the mirror is unreachable. Add `-s -- beta` (or a version such as `-s -- 5.1.1`) after `bash` to pick another channel. Windows CMD, fixing your `PATH`, updating and uninstalling are covered at [omo.dev/docs/install](https://omo.dev/docs/install). Prefer a package manager? `bun add -g omo-ai` (or `npm i -g omo-ai`) installs the same OmO. The package is `omo-ai`; the unrelated `omo` package on npm is someone else's. Open your project, run `omo`, describe the job. That's the whole setup. In a session, `/thinking ` sets how hard the model thinks (`/thinking` alone opens a picker), `Shift+Tab` cycles through the levels, and `/efforts ` sets the reasoning effort directly on models with effort grades. To pick up earlier work, `/resume` (or `/sessions`) opens your past sessions; from the shell, `omo -c` continues the last one and `omo -r` opens the picker. `/help` lists everything else. Coming from the OpenCode edition or LazyCodex? Run `omo setup` once. It carries your provider keys, custom providers, MCP servers, skills and model picks across. `omo doctor` then shows which task categories your providers can run and what the old install left behind, and `omo doctor --models` shows which model each category and agent runs and in what order (keep one out everywhere with [`exclude_models`](docs/reference/omo-json.md#exclude_models-native-harness)). The full walkthrough is [Migrating from OpenCode](docs/guide/migrating-from-opencode.md). To update, run the install line again (a package-manager install updates with `omo update`). `rm ~/.local/bin/omo` removes the binary install; `bun remove -g omo-ai` (or `npm uninstall -g omo-ai`) removes the package install. ## Why OmO **ultrawork.** Skip the study. If a task feels hard, add `ultrawork` (or `ulw`) to your prompt. The agent reads the codebase before touching a line, plans, proves each step before moving on, checks the result on the real surface, and stops when it's done. **Hundreds of agents, one keyword.** Type `mass ulw` and the whole job becomes a graph of agents: deep research over thousands of sources, a full machine-learning pipeline, a migration nobody wants to do. Each part runs on the model that fits it, in parallel, and gets checked before anything is called done. **Kibitzer. Your agent doesn't forget you, or your work.** Memory lives in a git repository of markdown files. A small, cheap model sits beside the expensive main agent, reads what you've done before, and nudges the main agent before it repeats a mistake. You stop re-explaining yourself. **Mix models without thinking about it.** Use the frontier models you love together with the cheap ones. Just sign in: `/login` covers Claude, ChatGPT, Kimi and GLM subscriptions. Every model ships with a system prompt tuned for it, so you never pick the wrong one. **High-quality skills, only the ones you need.** Your model is smart, but it still doesn't know a lot about solving real-world problems. OmO ships the missing knowledge as skills, browser use included, and loads only what the task needs. **Everything else is crafted.** Independent tool calls run together in one small program, so twenty reads are one round trip. Malformed tool arguments are repaired before they run. Waiting on a build or a deploy is a subscription, not polling. Long work keeps a record of what was checked, so a restarted session picks up where it stopped. Config, skills and prompts reload live. ## Configuration Opinionated defaults, adjustable if you insist. Your settings live in `~/.omo/omo.jsonc`, and a project can add its own `.omo/omo.jsonc`; the closest file wins. Every key is in the [configuration reference](docs/reference/configuration.md). ## Docs - [omo.dev/docs](https://omo.dev/docs) - [Migrating from OpenCode](docs/guide/migrating-from-opencode.md) - [Configuration reference](docs/reference/configuration.md) - [Features](docs/reference/features.md) - [Computer use](docs/guide/computer-use.md) (experimental) - [Ultrawork Manifesto](docs/manifesto.md) ## Reporting a bug The fastest way to report a bug is `/bug` inside a session (available in the omo app). It lists what it includes and lets you see the exact report before you send it, then sends it to the OmO team: the recent engine log, your environment and config with secrets blanked, the session transcript, and identity lines - your device name and, when telemetry is on, an install id and a session hash, plus your account details (email, name, account, user and device ids, plan, device name) when you report from the desktop app, so we can reply. Everything but the identity lines goes through the upload redactor. GitHub issues stay open for anyone who cannot use the in-app report. ## Reviews > "It made me cancel my Cursor subscription. Unbelievable things are happening in the open source community." - [Arthur Guiot](https://x.com/arthur_guiot/status/2008736347092382053?s=20) > "If Claude Code does in 7 days what a human does in 3 months, OmO does it in 1 hour."
- B, Quant Researcher > "You guys should pull this into core and recruit him. Seriously. It's really, really, really good."
- Henning Kilset ## Author's Note When I have to take the wheel back from an agent, that isn't teamwork. The system failed. OmO is built on that idea. You say what you want; the agent researches, plans, writes code you couldn't tell from a senior engineer's, verifies it, and keeps going until it's finished. It spends tokens when they buy real speed and routes the easy parts to cheap models. I'm this project's most obsessive user. Which model has the sharpest logic? Who writes the best prose? What did everyone else ship this week? OmO is where those answers land. Have a better way? PRs welcome. The goal is an agent you stop noticing. You flip the switch, the light turns on. The long version is the [Ultrawork Manifesto](docs/manifesto.md). No affiliation with any project or model mentioned. The Ultragoal and UltraQA ideas come from [oh-my-codex](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-codex), reimplemented from concept for OmO. ## Loved by professionals at [Indent](https://indentcorp.com), makers of Spray (influencer marketing solution), vovushop (cross-border commerce platform) and vreview (AI commerce review marketing solution). [Google](https://google.com). [Microsoft](https://microsoft.com). [Vercel](https://vercel.com). [ELESTYLE](https://elestyle.jp), makers of elepay (multi-mobile payment gateway) and OneQR (mobile application SaaS for cashless solutions). [Deepgram](https://deepgram.com).

The full walkthrough is Migrating from OpenCode.

To update, run the install line again (a package-manager install updates with omo update). rm ~/.local/bin/omo removes the binary install; bun remove -g omo-ai (or npm uninstall -g omo-ai) removes the package install.

Why OmO

Kibitzer. Your agent doesn't forget you, or your work. Memory lives in a git repository of markdown files. A small, cheap model sits beside the expensive main agent, reads what you've done before, and nudges the main agent before it repeats a mistake. You stop re-explaining yourself.

releases.name: v5.1.51
releases.body:
5.1.49 and 5.1.50 were not published; their changes ship here.

Session startup and task RPC attachment no longer wait for task-host liveness probes. Recovery runs independently per host, stops claiming or reviving children after shutdown, and preserves newer ownership claims. ([#11335](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11335)) DAG recovery and workpool reconciliation now wait for that same session-start reconcile (one shared gate) without holding admission, so a paused DAG's revivable child is never judged orphaned and a queued workpool item of an orphaned worker is redelivered rather than marked delivery_uncertain. ([#11525](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11525))

Continuing a synchronous task whose session was already deleted now fails at once with an error saying to start a new task, instead of waiting out the 30-minute sync poll timeout; a sync poll also stops when the server keeps reporting its session as not found. Completed sync task sessions now honor `background_task.taskCleanupDelayMs` instead of a fixed 10 minutes. Reported by @orgito. ([#11524](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11524), fixes [#11520](https://g

releases.name: v5.1.48
releases.body:
**OmO Native stops waiting on a stalled turn-end subscriber after two seconds.** Memory recovery remains retryable without treating the cancelled wait as a failed reflection run, and stall diagnostics identify the component and hook instead of only `omo.js`. Thanks to @floweredao for the report. ([#11254](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11254), Part of [#11249](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/11249)) ([#11280](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11280))

**Warm memory prompts avoid repeated git processes for HEAD and agreements.** Committed agreement reads are cached by repository and full revision, and cache misses inspect only the ledger path. Standard file-backed HEADs resolve from stat-validated Git files, including packed refs and linked worktrees, with git fallback for unusual layouts. ([#11216](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11216), part of [#10707](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/10707)) ([#11280](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11280))

releases.name: v5.1.46
releases.body:
**OmO Native init-deep committed mode no longer dead-ends.** Committed mode now finishes through its own pull-request handoff instead of pointing at a skill that does not ship with OmO Native, and it reports how to finish by hand when no PR can be opened. Thanks to @HolisticDeveloper for the report and @surlymochan for the fix. ([#11228](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11228), fixes [#9686](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/9686))

**The stale-reflection-lock test leaves no background writer behind when removing its temporary root.** Its teardown closes the memory wiring and awaits facts reconciliation and maintenance before removal, so a late lock publication cannot recreate the directory and make the temp-leak guard blame another test. ([#11225](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/11225))

**ulw-research ships a Markdown block model for checking Markdown and post deliverables.** It splits a Markdown report into headings, paragraphs, list items, table rows, code blocks and quotes with exact text offsets, and sorts sections with the same classifier as the HTML checks; an unclosed code fence is reported instead of passing si

releases.name: v5.1.45
releases.body:
**Reading the end of a long session takes 42 ms and 68 MB instead of 40 s and 1.8 GB.** `session_read`, `session_search` and `session_info` page through OpenCode's message API instead of loading the whole session: on a 23,000-message session, `session_read` with `limit: 2, from_end: true` dropped from 39.6 s and 1,848 MB peak memory to 42 ms and 68 MB, and a search that runs out its 60-second timeout now stops reading when it returns, where it used to read another 228 MB in the background ([#10738](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/10738), [#10741](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10741)).

**OmO's extension no longer carries an LSP engine it never runs.** The native LSP tools and post-edit diagnostics already go through the packaged LSP daemon, but the formatter's import pulled lsp-core's whole in-process engine into `omo.js`; importing only the helpers it uses shrinks the extension by about 82 KB, with no change in behavior. ([#10659](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10659))

aiSummary.oneLiner: A powerful TUI harness and orchestrator for coding agents like Codex and OpenCode, optimized for complex codebases.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: oh-my-opencode (also known as LazyCodex) provides an advanced terminal user interface (TUI) and orchestration harness for AI coding agents. It is designed specifically to manage complex codebases by handling context effectively for models like Codex and OpenCode. The tool is currently undergoing a major refactor to support a multi-harness OS, allowing seamless switching between different agent backends. It emphasizes real-time, transparent building, with the maintainer actively streaming development using their own AI assistant. The project aims to provide the ultimate 'token-maximizing' environment for power users.
keyFeatures: Advanced terminal interface: Offers a rich, interactive TUI for managing agent interactions directly from the command line.
Multi-harness architecture: Supports seamless switching between different AI backends like OpenCode, Codex, and Pi.
Complex codebase management: Specifically engineered to handle large repositories by optimizing context windows and token usage.
Real-time public development: Maintained publicly using an AI assistant, ensuring transparency and rapid iteration.
Easy installation: Provides a simple npx command for quick deployment without complex local configuration.
Extensible orchestration: Acts as a central operating system for managing various specialized coding agents and skills.

useCases.title: Large repository navigation
useCases.description: Use the optimized context handling to ask questions and generate code within massive, intricate enterprise codebases.

useCases.title: Multi-model experimentation
useCases.description: Easily swap between Codex, OpenCode, and other agent harnesses to compare performance on specific coding tasks.

useCases.title: Terminal-based AI coding
useCases.description: Interact with powerful coding agents entirely within the terminal, maintaining workflow without switching to a graphical IDE.

useCases.title: Agent orchestration
useCases.description: Manage and coordinate multiple specialized AI assistants to tackle different aspects of a software project simultaneously.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Terminal power users, AI researchers, and developers managing complex codebases who need a robust, terminal-native agent harness. It is ideal for 'token-maxxers' who want granular control over how their AI assistants consume and generate code.
